name: Middle Niger: a figure without a known biography
geographicPrecision: Broad regional/city orientation. No controlled excavation of this specimen is established in the released record.

interval.label: Thirteenth century CE
interval.note: Object catalogue date; not the foundation or abandonment of the city or the lifespan of its people.

question: Can urban life be studied without assuming a centralized state?
summary: A skilled clay figure and an excavated city answer different questions. Looking closely reveals a maker’s choices; settlement layers reveal food, building and craft work without recovering the figure’s lost biography.

sections.title: A maker’s choices remain visible
sections.text: A clay body bends around a raised knee; the head rests sideways, and arms draw the composition together. The back view shows raised oval forms and rows of small depressions. These are choices made in shaping a terracotta figure. Its maker gave a compact object a complicated posture. The museum dates it to the thirteenth century, but neither posture nor markings identify a named sitter, a feeling, an illness or a particular ritual. The broad Inland Niger Delta attribution does not supply a controlled excavation context.

sections.title: Food and materials supported urban life
sections.text: Jenné-jeno’s archaeology reaches far earlier than this object. Roderick and Susan McIntosh’s 1981 article describes a town growing among other settlements, with an urban high point around 750–1100. Its account connects rice, fish and fish oil with the region’s economy, alongside exchanged materials. People sustaining a town needed food as well as objects arriving from elsewhere. This makes cultivation, fishing and provisioning part of the urban story; imported valuables alone do not explain how a large community lived.

citations.locator: Exposed Extract: settlements, staples and exchange

sections.title: Places for work changed
sections.text: Later excavation reporting distinguishes domestic, burial and craft uses in different places and periods. Houses and granaries point to building and storage; furnace concentrations mark work involving heat. Dating showed that the sampled furnace areas were not all used together. A present-day scatter therefore cannot simply become a picture of simultaneous specialist neighborhoods. Reading the sequence helps recover people making and remaking places, rather than freezing the region at the date of the figure.

citations.locator: PDF pp. 4–7: changing uses and non-simultaneous activity

sections.title: Organization is a question to investigate
sections.text: The Met’s Sahel essay presents McIntosh’s interpretation of urbanism without centralized state hierarchy. That is an argument to assess, not proof that everyone was equal or that leadership was absent. A figure, a household deposit and a settlement survey offer different scales of evidence. Keeping those scales distinct makes room for forms of cooperation that a single royal biography could obscure.

deeperReading.title: What survives affects the comparison
deeperReading.text: The excavation report found limited variation in imported materials across sampled units and considered what that might mean for wealth. The authors also note that valuable textiles might not have survived. Erosion removed parts of the later occupation. A measure made from surviving imports cannot settle every kind of inequality, and an absent deposit may reflect loss rather than an unused place. The report’s proposed connection between Jenné-jeno’s decline and Djenné’s growth likewise remains a hypothesis, not an established movement of every household.

deeperReading.title: Knowledge of a place has living custodians
deeperReading.text: In a 2020 interview, Malian archaeologist Daouda Keïta stresses local knowledge of land, accessible accounts and community participation in caring for heritage. He also calls for critical comparison between oral histories and archaeological remains. His published account was translated and edited from French. It offers an attributed perspective on how research should work, not a statement made by every community or an explanation of this particular figure. The Met’s 1981 purchase credit adds a modern acquisition date; it does not reconstruct the object’s earlier custody or an ancient owner.

evidenceReading.title: A visible form, a dated sequence and an attributed voice
evidenceReading.introduction: These are editorial paraphrases and interpretations of different sources, not quotations or newly recovered information about a named person.

items.label: Object photograph and catalogue
items.text: The photographs show a bent body and patterned back. The catalogue identifies terracotta and a thirteenth-century date, while offering possible readings of the posture.
items.interpretation: A visible detail can support a precise description without proving an emotion, diagnosis or use. The catalogue narrative’s Jenne-jeno attribution is not a recorded excavation locus for this specimen.

items.label: Furnaces need a sequence
items.text: The excavation report discusses furnace concentrations at several mound sites. Its dating results indicate that these activity areas were not simultaneous.
items.interpretation: Spatial separation alone cannot establish a single contemporary system of specialist districts. Chronology changes the organization that can reasonably be inferred.

items.label: An archaeologist’s account of collaboration
items.text: Keïta’s 2020 interview links knowledge of land and heritage care with the participation of local communities; he asks researchers to compare oral sources critically with material evidence.
items.interpretation: This is a named, translated and edited modern perspective. It does not supply universal community approval, a medieval constitution or the missing biography of Met accession 1981.218.

familyActivity.title: Describe, compare, leave room
steps: Look at the front and back views. Describe two shapes or marks without giving the person a feeling, a name or a diagnosis.

Read this source capsule: the museum dates the figure to the thirteenth century. Excavated settlement traces include houses, granaries and furnace areas, but the sampled furnace areas were not all used at once. The figure has no established controlled findspot in those excavations.
Complete two sentences: “The photographs show …” and “The settlement evidence suggests work such as …”. Then name one question that neither source answers about this person-shaped object.
familyActivity.explanation: A head resting against a knee and raised marks are visible. Building, storing food and working with heat come from the supplied archaeology capsule, not from the posture. Who made the figure, why it was made and what the person represents remain open. Different evidence can explain a place without inventing an individual life.

review.reviewer: Codex selected source consultation and internal author checking; not independent historian, Malian community or conservator approval
review.scope: A bounded reading: the unchanged object is paired with selected excavator reporting and an attributed Malian archaeological perspective. The complete original case interval, claims, object order, dimensions, identity, coordinates, image metadata and pixels remain preserved. The added reference is a separate selected archaeological frame.
limitations: The object’s controlled findspot, original function, maker, sitter, earlier custody and modern photographic date remain unestablished. Catalogue emotion/illness suggestions are not diagnoses or adopted biography.

The 1981 paper was read only through its exposed extract. The selected Rice report has an uncertain surviving version/publication date; its fieldwork, conference and cited-publication dates remain distinct. Underlying full monographs and field records were not consulted.

Modern furnace/household interpretations are sampled and dated; no single simultaneous, ethnic or occupational district plan is reconstructed. The colonial dispensary labor discussion is outside the medieval account.

The inherited entry noted differing institutional endings for Jenné-jeno. This selected consultation did not freshly establish a second ending: the inspected excavation report and current Met text use by 1400. Neither dates the figure or a population’s disappearance.

Keïta’s interview is translated and edited; no original French recording/transcript or universal community endorsement checked. Fresh provenance-tab consultation was unavailable after the recorded access failure. No new media, surveyed locator, route, source plan or annotation is supplied.
